principle_text: When the seller offers additional items along with the main product, avoid providing vague budget constraints without specifying a concrete lower offer to prevent weakening your negotiation leverage.
When the seller is willing to negotiate and offers additional value, you should anchor the negotiation with your target price to pressure the seller to move towards a more favorable price.
When the seller deflects with non-serious responses to buyer inquiries, avoid asking casual questions that do not directly negotiate price terms to prevent weakening your leverage in the negotiation.

When the seller shows willingness to reduce their initial price, you should directly propose your target price to establish a clear starting point for negotiation and signal progress towards a better deal.

When the seller shows willingness to negotiate and lowers their counteroffer, you should introduce additional conditions like in-person pickup to justify a lower price and move closer to your target price.
When the seller has already reduced the price to $465 and is hesitant to go lower, you should continue negotiating to push for a lower price rather than accepting the offer immediately.
When the seller acknowledges minor scratches on a vintage item, avoid immediately pushing for a price reduction based on this information without further negotiation or justification.
When the seller confirms the good condition of the item, avoid asking questions that do not directly address price negotiation, such as inquiring about the item's previous usage environment.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate by offering a lower price with added value, you should consider accepting the revised offer to reach a mutually beneficial agreement.
When the seller shows openness to a deal at an increased price without conceding anything additional, avoid conceding to the seller's counteroffer too quickly to maintain leverage in negotiation.
When the seller has already made a counteroffer and the buyer offers a slightly lower amount, consider accepting the revised offer to close the deal with a price closer to the buyer's target.

When the seller has already accepted the buyer's offer and the negotiation is concluded, avoid making celebratory or redundant statements that do not contribute to further price reduction or negotiation progress.

When the seller has an item listed for $40 and mentions its excellent condition, avoid conceding by offering a higher price than your initial target and implying willingness to pay more than the original asking price.

When the seller focuses on product features rather than price, avoid asking questions that do not directly advance the price negotiation, to ensure the conversation stays on track towards reaching a mutually beneficial agreement.
When the buyer establishes credibility as a repeat customer, you should consider lowering the price slightly to show flexibility and accommodate their needs.
When the seller has already made a price concession, you should accept the offer to secure a better deal and avoid risking losing the opportunity for further negotiation.
When the seller emphasizes the item's value and new condition, avoid making significantly low offers that undermine your negotiating leverage.

When the seller introduces additional items to the deal instead of lowering the price in response to buyer's depreciation argument, it weakens the buyer's leverage by shifting focus away from price reduction and towards immediate purchase with added items.

When the seller offers additional items as part of a deal, avoid rejecting them outright without attempting to negotiate the main item's price down, as it can weaken your leverage and be perceived as unreasonable.

When the seller has already reduced their initial price in response to buyer's negotiation tactics, you should continue to apply value references and cost negotiation to further improve your position.
When the seller has already offered a price and not budging, avoid making unrelated comments about personal convenience or transportation methods that do not directly impact the price negotiation.
When the seller offers a price close to the buyer's initial target, avoid unilaterally reducing your offer below your own initial price as it may weaken your negotiation leverage.
When the seller offers a discount and free delivery, avoid accepting the counteroffer without further negotiation to prevent weakening your position and leverage in the price negotiation.
When the seller has already agreed to a lower price and a condition like self-pickup, avoid accepting the condition without attempting to negotiate for a further price reduction.
When the seller emphasizes the newness of the item and justifies the price based on recent purchase, you should reference market prices to negotiate a lower offer effectively.
When the seller indicates the item is basically brand-new and just doesn't work for them, you should negotiate for added benefits like a drop-off service to enhance your leverage in the negotiation.
When the seller has already agreed to a price, avoid accepting the offer without attempting to further negotiate for a better deal to prevent settling on a higher final price.
When the seller emphasizes product features like quality and included accessories, avoid shifting focus away from price negotiation by asking about additional details unrelated to price.
When the seller affirms the item's excellent condition, avoid asking about potential flaws as it may inadvertently weaken your negotiation position by removing leverage points.
When the buyer firmly proposes their initial offer and expresses enthusiasm for the item, the seller should show willingness to negotiate by adjusting the price closer to the buyer's target.
When the seller offers to meet you in the middle, avoid accepting the counteroffer without further negotiation to prevent finalizing the deal at a less favorable price than your target.
When the seller confirms the item's pristine condition, avoid asking generic questions about scratches or dings that do not directly impact price negotiation.
When the seller emphasizes the item's quality and condition, you should gradually increase your offer to signal willingness to negotiate while maintaining leverage.
When the seller has previously countered with a price lower than the initial asking price, you should propose a midpoint price to secure a better deal and avoid further haggling.
When the seller emphasizes the heavy piece in perfect condition, avoid proposing a significantly lower price without acknowledging the value of the item, as it may risk undermining the negotiation.
When the seller offers to include additional features like LED lights in the negotiation, you should increase your initial offer slightly to create leverage for securing a better deal.

When the seller has already offered a discounted price and additional item, you should show willingness to compromise and add a personal commitment to strengthen your position, leading to a successful negotiation outcome.
When the seller has already accepted a price offer, avoid reconfirming the deal without introducing new negotiation tactics or altering terms, as it does not impact leverage or deal progression.
When the seller offers a slightly higher price including shipping, you should accept the combined offer to secure free shipping and finalize the deal efficiently.
When the seller agrees to specific improvements tied to a higher offer, you should leverage critiques of item descriptions to negotiate price reductions linked to added value.
When the seller responds to a buyer's inquiry with vague or irrelevant product details, avoid asking questions that do not directly relate to price or negotiation leverage.

When the seller provides vague or weak justification for a premium price, you should persistently inquire for specific details to undermine their claim and strengthen your position to negotiate a lower price.
When the seller maintains a firm but negotiable price, you should make a lower counteroffer to create downward pressure and encourage the seller to concede closer to your target price.

When the seller indicates a firm minimum price but shows willingness to negotiate, you should present a reasonable compromise that leverages product value concerns and your own constraints to encourage acceptance.
When the seller has already accepted your target price, avoid making additional offers or requests that do not contribute to improving the deal.

When the seller responds to a low initial offer with a counteroffer close to the buyer's target price, you should make an aggressive lower counteroffer to create downward price pressure and encourage concessions.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer between their initial price and your offer, you should accept promptly to secure a better deal and avoid unnecessary prolonging of negotiation.

When the seller holds firm on a higher price and emphasizes the item's value and condition, you should avoid highlighting minor inconveniences that may justify the asking price and instead focus on negotiating from a position of informed value.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer after your initial concession, you should justify your lower offer with practical reasons to maintain leverage and encourage further price reduction.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer below their initial price, you should accept the offer to reach a successful compromise and secure a better deal.
When the seller makes a price concession in response to a buyer's practical concern, you should leverage that concern to request a further price reduction.
When the seller makes a moderate concession but the price gap remains large, you should firmly restate your lower offer to pressure the seller into a more significant price reduction.
When the seller firmly states a minimum acceptable price, avoid increasing your offer and adding extra non-monetary concessions without securing a price reduction.
When the seller firmly holds a minimum price and rejects additional concessions, avoid signaling disengagement without proposing new offers or concessions, as it may weaken your negotiation leverage.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate price and emphasizes the item's value, you should combine a lower offer with added value to increase your leverage and encourage acceptance.
When the seller responds with a flexible but anchored price range, avoid vague requests for price reduction without specifying a target amount or justification.
When the seller signals a firm price range but shows openness to negotiation, you should make a bold, low offer combined with an emotional appeal to encourage a significant price concession.
When the seller offers a counterproposal with added value and a reduced price, you should accept the offer promptly to finalize the deal efficiently.
When the seller confirms product functionality and adds value without lowering price, avoid focusing solely on non-price features that do not create leverage for a better price.
When the seller confirms the item's condition but the buyer identifies a missing feature that affects value, you should highlight this gap to create leverage for negotiating a better price.

When the seller counters a low buyer offer by moderately lowering their price and offering added convenience, you should justify your offer with additional costs to pressure the seller toward a better deal.
When the seller makes a clear and reasonable counteroffer that improves on your initial price, you should accept it promptly to secure a favorable deal and avoid losing the opportunity.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer closer to their listing price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage for a better deal.
When the seller repeats existing item details without offering new information, avoid asking questions that do not increase negotiation leverage or prompt price concessions.
When the seller firmly justifies a high price with credible market comparisons, avoid making offers that are drastically lower than your initial price as it weakens your negotiating position.
When the seller firmly rejects a low offer and sets a higher fixed price, avoid conceding too quickly as it may strengthen the seller's position and reduce your negotiation leverage.
When the seller firmly holds a higher price and rejects lower offers, avoid conceding too quickly with midpoint offers that can empower the seller to raise the price or add unfavorable conditions.
When the seller has made a clear final price concession, avoid making lower offers combined with new demands that can weaken your negotiation leverage.

When the seller acknowledges the item's value but expresses willingness to negotiate and invites your offer, you should introduce conditional incentives like immediate cash payment to encourage price concessions.

When the seller shows willingness to negotiate but maintains a firm price, you should anchor the negotiation with a specific lower offer that acknowledges the seller's position to prompt a better counteroffer.
When the seller reaffirms the product's quality and justifies the asking price without conceding, avoid asking questions that do not directly advance your position toward a price reduction.
When the seller confirms product details without adjusting price or terms, avoid asking questions that do not advance price negotiation or create leverage.

When the seller shows willingness to negotiate but sets a firm lower limit, you should introduce competitive alternatives and emphasize your readiness to close quickly to create leverage for a better price.

When the seller makes a firm but negotiable counteroffer with a minimum acceptable price, you should respond with a justified lower offer that highlights your constraints to encourage further price reduction.
When the seller clearly states their lowest acceptable price and offers a small concession, you should accept the reasonable final offer to close the deal efficiently.
When the seller admits minor imperfections but confirms full functionality, you should probe the item's condition to uncover leverage for negotiating a lower price.

When the seller makes a moderate price concession from their initial asking price, you should present a significantly lower offer combined with immediate purchase intent to increase leverage and encourage further price reductions.
When the seller makes a firm counteroffer close to your target price, you should respond with a specific, slightly lower counteroffer to encourage further concessions.
When the seller makes a clear and final price offer, you should signal acceptance promptly to secure a favorable deal and conclude the negotiation efficiently.
When the seller confirms product completeness or included components, avoid asking purely factual questions that do not advance price negotiation or create leverage.
When the seller resists lowering the base price and offers non-price concessions instead, avoid accepting alternatives that do not directly reduce the price.
When the seller offers additional items instead of lowering the price, avoid accepting extras without negotiating a lower base price to maintain leverage in price negotiation.

When the seller firmly maintains their original asking price without concession, avoid lowering your offer below your initial price as it weakens your negotiating leverage without prompting seller movement.

When the seller firmly maintains a high price for brand new items, avoid making minimal price increases combined with justifications that reduce your purchase quantity, as this weakens your bargaining leverage.
When the seller offers a conditional price reduction tied to buyer actions, you should leverage your resale intentions or use specific buyer needs to prompt concessions closer to your target price.

When the seller has made a firm counteroffer that includes specific concessions like pickup, avoid making only marginal price increases with additional minor conditions that weaken your bargaining position.

When the seller confirms the item's condition and details without indicating price flexibility, avoid focusing solely on information-gathering questions that do not create leverage for price negotiation.
When the seller rejects a low offer but counters with a higher price and additional conditions, avoid making an initial offer that is too low and far from your target price.
When the seller firmly states their minimum price and delivery terms upfront, avoid conceding on price while requesting additional services that the seller has explicitly refused.
When the seller clearly states non-negotiable terms such as no delivery despite ad content, avoid challenging these terms without presenting a new offer or leverage to influence the price.
When the seller makes a counteroffer above the buyer's initial price, avoid immediately accepting it without further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller sets a firm final price, avoid immediately matching it with additional requests that add value to the seller, as this reduces your leverage in price negotiation.
When the seller has agreed to a price and pickup arrangement, avoid ending the negotiation without attempting to explore any additional value or terms.
When the seller indicates willingness to negotiate price for a bulk purchase, you should propose buying multiple items to leverage a better overall deal.
When the seller sets a firm minimum price citing cost concerns, you should emphasize immediate purchase and cash payment while making a lower counteroffer to encourage price reduction.
When the seller clearly states their lowest acceptable price, avoid setting a firm maximum offer below that price without proposing compromises or emphasizing added value to keep negotiations open.
When the seller shows willingness to lower the price quickly, you should make a strong counteroffer below your initial budget to secure a better deal immediately.
When the seller has just agreed to your price offer without further concessions, avoid shifting focus to logistical details that do not influence the price negotiation leverage.

When the seller indicates willingness to negotiate under specific conditions, you should make a specific counteroffer that incorporates those conditions to effectively pressure the seller to lower their price.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer close to your target price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to improve your deal.
When the seller justifies their price by referencing their original cost, avoid responding with non-substantive greetings that fail to engage with price discussions or budget inquiries.
When the seller counters a low offer by adding extra services that increase the price, avoid accepting offers that effectively raise your total cost beyond your initial budget.

When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer below their initial price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller confirms the item is in excellent condition without price concessions, avoid asking irrelevant questions that do not directly support negotiating a lower price.
When the seller emphasizes the high quality and unique origin of the item's materials, avoid asking questions that allow the seller to reinforce the product's value and justify a higher price.
When the seller states a firm price, you should clearly express your budget constraints and request a price reduction to encourage the seller to offer a lower, negotiable price.
When the seller offers a price reduction with additional conditions, you should propose a slightly lower price without accepting those conditions to encourage immediate acceptance.

When the seller partially concedes on price but holds firm on their value, you should propose a specific discount combined with a convenience offer to anchor the negotiation closer to your target price.
When the seller clearly states a firm counteroffer with specific conditions, you should clarify and confirm the terms explicitly to demonstrate understanding and move the negotiation forward.
When the seller makes a clear, lowered counteroffer including added value like delivery, you should accept the offer promptly to finalize the deal and secure a better price.
When the seller reiterates the price without addressing the buyer's informational question, avoid ignoring the buyer's attempts to gather details that could support negotiation.
When the seller reiterates the item's high value and condition without lowering the price, avoid repeating previously asked questions that allow the seller to reinforce their price justification.

When the seller provides a justification based on item condition comparing it to brand new, you should challenge vague claims by requesting precise information to leverage depreciation in price negotiation.
When the seller emphasizes urgency to sell quickly, you should anchor your offer by highlighting product limitations and maintenance costs to justify a significantly lower price.
